evals.prompt: Teach me how backpropagation works. I write code for a living but I've never done any machine learning.
evals.expected_output: A structured, interactive lesson that starts by sketching a knowledge framework, then confirms the goal, probes the learner's boundary, and presents a learning plan before teaching backpropagation.
expectations: Starts by drawing a big-picture knowledge framework before asking anything
Clarifies the learning goal via ask_user with multiple-choice options
Probes the cognitive boundary (code-yes, ML-no) via ask_user with multiple-choice options
Presents a learning plan as a diagram and confirms before teaching
Explains new concepts by building on prior knowledge rather than dumping facts
Asks only one question per message, mostly multiple choice, never yes/no

evals.prompt: I use git every day — add, commit, push, branch — but I don't actually understand how commits and branches work under the hood. Help me really get it.
evals.expected_output: An interactive walkthrough that maps out git's conceptual model, finds where the user's mental model stops, plans a path, and teaches the underlying model step by step.
expectations: Begins with a knowledge framework (big picture) of how git works
Uses ask_user to confirm the specific goal rather than assuming
Locates the boundary between rote commands and real understanding
Draws a learning-plan diagram ≤120 chars per line before teaching
Checks understanding after each goal, one question at a time, no yes/no questions

evals.prompt: Explain quantum entanglement to me. I remember high school physics — atoms, electrons, energy levels — but nothing beyond that.
evals.expected_output: A lesson that builds from the learner's high-school physics, mapping the conceptual path to entanglement and confirming the plan before diving in.
expectations: Starts from the stated boundary (high-school physics) rather than assuming more
Sketches a framework showing where entanglement sits among related concepts
Confirms the learning goal and plan with the user before teaching
Uses diagrams to convey relationships, keeping lines ≤120 characters
Uses plain numbering and avoids hard-to-distinguish symbols such as circled numbers
